en: Bhartṛhari: *Śatakatraya* (1. *Nītiśataka*, 2. *Śṛṅgāraśataka*, 3. *Vairāgyaśataka*)
The Century of Ethics by Bhartṛhari:
To Him whose form is infinite pure consciousness, unconditioned by space, time, and the like;
Homage to the peaceful splendor, for whom self-experience alone is the sole authority.
Those who understand [the truth] are seized by envy;
those in power are defiled by pride;
and others are struck down by ignorance.
Sublime speech has withered within his body. (BharŚt 1.2)
An ignorant person is easily pleased;
one who possesses specialized knowledge is even more easily pleased; but one who is puffed up by a mere fragment of knowledge is difficult to satisfy.
Even Brahmā does not delight that man.
One might forcibly extract a jewel from between the fangs of a makara’s mouth, cross even the ocean agitated by rows of surging waves,
or carry even an enraged serpent upon one's head like a flower.
But one should not seek to please the minds of foolish people who are obstinately attached [to their views]. // BharSt_1.4 //
One might obtain oil from sand even by pressing it with great effort;
one tormented by thirst might drink water from mirages;
or while wandering somewhere, one might find the horn of a hare.
But one should not seek to please the mind of a stubborn fool. // BharSt_1.5 //
He strives to restrain a fierce beast with the fibers of a young lotus stalk;
he prepares to cleave a diamond-gem with the tip of a *śirīṣa* flower;
he seeks to produce sweetness from a drop of honey in the salt ocean.
They desire to lead the wicked onto the path of the virtuous by means of their well-spoken words, which distill the essence of nectar.
The covering of ignorance, which is entirely virtuous and dependent solely upon oneself, was fashioned by the Creator;
for this reason, it is especially appropriate in the assembly of all-knowing ones.
Silence is the ornament of the unlearned.
When I was a knower of only a little, like an elephant blinded by rut,
my mind became arrogant, thinking "I am omniscient";
but when I understood even a small portion from the presence of wise men...
Then, like a fever, my intoxication vanished with the thought, "I am a fool. (BharSt 1.8)

A dog, with a mind like a swarm of worms, greedily eats a human bone— foul-smelling, loathsome, and drenched in saliva— finding incomparable pleasure in it even though it is devoid of flesh; yet, seeing even the Lord of the Gods standing nearby, he does not fear him.
For a base creature does not take account of the worthlessness of its possessions.
From the head of Śarva she went to heaven; from the head of Paśupati to the mountain;
from the lofty mountain to the earth; and from the earth to the ocean.
Thus, O Gaṅgā, you have descended lower and lower, step by step, little by little.
Alternatively, for those who have fallen away from discernment, there occurs a downfall with a hundred gates.
Fire can be warded off by water, the heat of the sun by an umbrella, a rutting lord of elephants by a sharp goad, and cattle or donkeys by a staff; likewise,
disease by the collection of various medicines, and poison by the application of mantras.
For everyone there is a medicine prescribed by the scriptures; for the fool, however, there is no remedy.
One devoid of literature, music, and the arts is a literal beast lacking tail and horns;
though living, such a person does not even consume grass.
That is the supreme lot of the sacrificial animals.
Those who possess neither learning nor austerity, neither generosity nor wisdom, neither virtue nor excellence, nor righteousness—
they are merely a burden upon the earth in the world of mortals.
Deer roam about in human form.
It is better to wander with forest-dwellers in the mountain fastnesses than to have contact with foolish people.
Even in the palaces of the lord of gods.
That ruler of the earth whose subjects— renowned poets whose speech is beautiful with words refined by the scriptures, who bestow the sacred traditions upon their disciples— live there impoverished,
is himself dull-witted; for poets are lords even without wealth.
For those who have depreciated the value of jewels are indeed contemptible bad examiners. (BharŚt 1.15)

The inner wealth known as knowledge never comes within the reach of a thief; it ever nourishes some inexplicable well-being; though constantly bestowed upon supplicants, it incessantly attains supreme increase; and even at the end of cosmic aeons, it does not go to its destruction.
O kings, abandon pride toward them; who can rival them?
Do not despise those wise ones who have realized the ultimate truth; fortune, as light as a blade of grass, cannot obstruct them—
those whose cheeks are darkened by the streaks of fresh rut.
A lotus fiber cannot serve as a restraint for elephants.
An enraged Creator utterly destroys the swan's graceful sport of dwelling in the lotus groves,
yet he does not destroy its celebrated skill in distinguishing milk from water.
He is capable of taking away the fame of one's cleverness. (Bharata Śāstra 1.18)
Armlets do not adorn a man, nor necklaces bright as the moon;
neither bathing, nor ointments, nor flowers, nor well-ornamented hair do so.
Speech alone adorns a man—speech that is refined and maintained.
Indeed, all ornaments wear away with time; but the ornament of speech is an ornament that never decays.
Knowledge is a man’s supreme form; knowledge is hidden and protected wealth;
knowledge provides enjoyment, fame, and happiness; knowledge is the teacher of teachers;
knowledge is a kinsman when traveling abroad; knowledge is the highest deity.
Knowledge is honored among kings, but wealth is not; one devoid of knowledge is a mere beast. (Bhartrihari Śataka 1.20)
If there is patience, what need is there for armor; if there is anger in embodied beings, what need for enemies?
If there is kinship, what need for fire; if there is a friend, what need for divine medicine? If there is faultless knowledge, what need for snakes or for wealth?
If there is modesty, what need is there for ornaments? If there is true poetry, what need is there for a kingdom? (Bhartrihari 1.21)
Courtesy toward one's kin, compassion for one's servants, constant guile toward the wicked, affection for the virtuous, statesmanship toward fellow kings, and straightforwardness toward the learned;
valor toward enemies, forbearance toward elders, and boldness toward one's beloved.
And upon those men who are thus skilled in the arts depends the stability of the world. (BharSt 1.22)
It removes dullness from the intellect, pours truth into speech, bestows the elevation of honor, and dispels evil;
it clarifies the mind and spreads one's fame in all directions.
Tell me, what does association with the virtuous not accomplish for men? (Bhartrihari Śataka 1.23)
Victorious are those masters of poetry, performers of good deeds who have attained mastery over aesthetic flavor (rasa), whose bodies of fame never perish.
The fear born of old age and death. // BharSt 1.24 //
A son of virtuous conduct, a devoted wife, a master inclined toward grace, an affectionate and honest friend, a retinue free from even a trace of affliction,
a handsome and stable form, wealth, and a face brightened by learning— [these are the blessings].
When Hari, the remover of the world's suffering, is pleased, that which is sought by embodied beings is attained.
Abstaining from taking life, restraint in seizing the wealth of others, truthful speech,

giving according to one's ability at the proper time, remaining mute regarding talk of young women, breaking the stream of craving for others' possessions, humility toward gurus, and compassion for all living beings.
This is the common path to the highest goods, whose method is unimpaired in all the scriptures. (BharSt 1.26)
The base indeed do not begin an undertaking out of fear of obstacles; the mediocre, having begun, desist when thwarted by obstacles;
but the noble, though struck again and again by obstacles, continue on.
Noble people do not abandon what they have begun. (Bhartrihari, Śatakatraya 1.27)

The wicked should not be entreated; even a friend who has meager wealth should not be asked for a favor; one’s livelihood should be righteous; and it is better to remain poor than to perform an ignoble act even at the cost of life.
In times of adversity, one should maintain a high station and follow the example of the great.
By whom was this perilous vow, which is like the edge of a sword, prescribed for the virtuous? (BharSt 1.28)

Though emaciated by hunger, though wasted by old age, though his vital strength was failing, and though he had fallen into a miserable state with his radiance extinguished— even as his life-breaths were perishing—
he maintained a single, fixed longing for a mouthful of flesh from the temples of a lordly elephant in rut.
Does the lion, the leader of those with great pride, eat withered grass? (BharSt 1.29)
A dog, having found even a bone of a cow that is fleshless, filthy, and has only a trace of sinew and fat remaining, attains satisfaction; yet that bone does not serve to appease its hunger.
A lion, however, abandons a jackal even when it has come into its very lap and slays an elephant instead.
Everyone, even when fallen into hardship, desires a reward that corresponds to their own nature.
A dog wags its tail, stamps its hind feet on the ground,
falls down, and reveals its mouth and belly to one who gives it food;
but an excellent elephant does not act in this way.
She gazes steadily at him and enjoys herself with hundreds of endearing words. (Bharata Śāstra 1.31)
In this ever-turning cycle of existence, who indeed does not die and not take birth?
He alone is truly born by whom, having been born, [the purpose of birth is fulfilled].
The lineage attains great eminence. // BharSt_1.32 //
Like a cluster of blossoms,
there are two possible courses for a high-minded man:
either to stand at the head of all the world, or to wither away.
Or it perishes right there in the forest.
There are also others, such as Bṛhaspati and five or six other esteemed ones; Rāhu does not harbor enmity toward them, for he delights in his extraordinary prowess.
He swallows only two luminaries, the lords of day and night.
"Brother, behold on this festival day the lord of the Dānavas, whose form now consists of nothing but his head."
Śeṣa bears the succession of worlds resting upon the surface of his hoods,
and he, in turn, is always supported on the middle of his back by the Lord of Tortoises;
yet the Ocean, with utter disregard, holds even him under its belly.
Ah! The manifestations of the deeds of the great are indeed boundless.

Ah, for the son of the Snowy Mountain, while his father was overwhelmed by distress, it would have been better to have one's wings severed by the blows of the thunderbolt released by the intoxicated Indra— blows heavy with the surging flames of a rising fire— than to endure such a fate.
And such a falling together as this is not appropriate for the ocean, the lord of waters, with [ordinary] water.
Even as a cub, a lion falls upon elephants whose temples are stained with rut;
such is the nature of those possessed of courage.
Indeed, age is not the cause of spiritual power. (BharSt 1.37)
Let my birth sink into the netherworld; let it go even deeper there along with its multitude of virtues.
Let my character fall from a mountain cliff; let my noble lineage be consumed by fire.
Let a thunderbolt swiftly strike down my valor as an enemy; let there be for us only wealth.
Without which single quality, all these other virtues are as insignificant as a mere fragment of straw. (Bharata Śāstra 1.38)
Acquire wealth, O descendant of Kakutstha;
this world has wealth as its root.
I perceive no difference between them.
And for one who has died without wealth. (Bhārataśāstra 1.39)
Those very senses remain unimpaired, that same name remains, that same intellect remains unobstructed, and those very words remain;
yet in an instant, a man is deprived of the warmth of wealth.
That too becomes something else entirely; this is truly extraordinary.
He who possesses wealth is a man of noble birth; he is a scholar, learned, and a connoisseur of virtues; he alone is an eloquent speaker and he is handsome to behold.
All virtues take refuge in gold.

A king perishes through bad counsel; an ascetic, through attachment; a son, through over-indulgence; a Brahmin, through neglecting his studies; a family, through a wicked son; character, through service to the base;
modesty, through liquor; agriculture, through lack of supervision; and affection, through residing abroad.
Friendship [is lost] through lack of affection, prosperity through misconduct, and wealth through wastefulness and negligence.
Giving, enjoyment, and loss— these are the three destinies of wealth for one who neither gives nor enjoys it.
For him, there is a third destiny. (BharSt 1.43)
A gem polished on a whetstone; an elephant victorious in battle, its pride exhausted by the blows of weapons; rivers with their sandy banks exposed in autumn;
the moon reduced to a single digit; and a young woman worn out by amorous play.
Bowing down before supplicants, men whose wealth has vanished shine with splendor. (Bhartrihari Śataka 1.44)
Someone who is destitute longs for a handful of barley; once he is later restored to full prosperity, he regards the entire earth as equal to a blade of grass.
Thus, because of this lack of certainty regarding the relative weight or lightness of objects among the wealthy, [one should not judge by outward appearances].
And state both expands and contracts objects. (BharSt 1.45)
O King, if you wish to milk this cow of the earth,
then nourish that other world today as if it were her calf; for when it is properly and constantly nourished, [the earth will yield its milk].
The earth bears fruit with various fruits, like a wish-fulfilling creeper.
She may be truthful or untruthful, harsh or sweet-spoken,
cruel or compassionate, devoted to wealth or generous; she may be constantly spending or possessed of abundant and constant income.
The policy of kings, like a courtesan, assumes many forms.
Command, fame, protection of the Brahmins,
charity, enjoyment, and the safeguarding of friends—
those in whom these six qualities do not prevail [are not true kings].
What purpose do they have in taking refuge with a king?
Whatever wealth— be it small or great— is inscribed by the Creator upon the tablet of one's own forehead,
that one obtains even in a desert, and not more than that even on Mount Meru; therefore,
be steadfast, and do not vainly adopt the miserable conduct of those who possess riches.
Observe that a jar draws an equal amount of water from both a well and the ocean. (Bhartrihari Śatakatraya 1.49)
Who does not know that you alone are the support of the cātaka birds?
What more can we, O best of clouds, say?
You wait for what is spoken out of miserliness.
O Cātaka bird, friend, listen for a moment with an attentive mind:
many clouds dwell in the sky, yet not all of them are like this;
some moisten the earth with their rains, while others merely thunder in vain.
Do not speak words of dejection in the presence of whomever you see.
Lack of compassion, engaging in conflict without cause, longing for the wealth and wives of others, and intolerance toward virtuous people and kinsmen.
For this is indeed innate to those of evil soul.
A wicked person should be avoided even if he is adorned with learning, just as a snake is not to be approached even if it is decorated with a jewel.
Is he not terrifying? (BharSt 1.53)

In one possessed of modesty, dullness is reckoned; in one who delights in vows, hypocrisy; in the pure, deceit; in the hero, cruelty; in the sage, lack of intellect; in the sweet-spoken, wretchedness;
in the brilliant, arrogance; in the eloquent, garrulousness; and in the steadfast, incapacity.
What indeed could be the merit of those possessing virtues that is not marred by the wicked? (Bhartrihari, Śatakatraya 1.54)
If there is greed, what is the use of virtue? If there is backbiting, what is the use of sins?
If there is truth, what is the use of austerity? If the mind is pure, what is the use of a sacred ford?
If there is goodness, what is the use of other qualities? If there is great majesty, what is the use of ornaments?
If one possesses the sixfold knowledge, what is the use of wealth? If there is infamy, what is the use of life? (BharSt 1.55)
The moon is pale during the day; a passionate woman has lost her youth; a lake is devoid of lotuses; a handsome face is without eloquence;
a master is devoted to wealth; and a virtuous person is perpetually destitute.
That wicked man who has entered the royal court causes seven thorns in my heart. (Bhartrihari Śataka 1.56)
To kings who are fierce in their wrath, no one is truly "one's own," not even a priest while he is offering oblations.
Fire carries [the offering] when it has been touched.
One who is silent like a mute yet eloquent in speech, or a chatterer who is arrogant;
one who dwells constantly at his side yet remains distant when lacking confidence;
one who is timid out of patience—if he does not endure these, he is generally not of noble birth.
The dharma of service is supremely profound, inaccessible even to yogins.
Of this one who has exposed all wicked people, who acts without restraint, whose own base course of action was previously expanded and manifested,
and who, by fate, has obtained power while being a hater of virtue—
Happiness is attained by those who have entered the sphere of the base. // BharSt_1.59 //
Heavy at its commencement, gradually diminishing, light at first and subsequently increasing—
thus is the day divided into its former and latter halves.
The friendship of the wicked and the virtuous is like a shadow.

In this world, hunters, fishermen, and slanderers are causeless enemies toward the deer, fish, and the virtuous, whose livelihoods are sustained by grass, water, and contentment respectively. (Bhartrihari Śatakatraya 1.61)
A desire for the company of the virtuous, affection for the virtues of others, humility toward one’s teacher, devotion to learning, attachment to one’s own wife, fear of public censure,
devotion to the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva), the power to subdue oneself, and avoidance of the wicked— [these are the marks of a noble soul].
Homage to those men in whom these stainless virtues dwell.
Fortitude in adversity, forbearance in prosperity,
eloquence in the assembly, valor in battle,
a love for fame, and devotion to sacred learning.
For this is indeed innate to the great-souled ones. (BharŚt 1.63)
Giving in secret; showing a display of hospitality when someone arrives at the house; maintaining silence after doing a kindness; speaking of one's favors in an assembly;
freedom from pride in prosperity; and stories about others that are devoid of any hint of disparagement.
By whom was this difficult vow, which is like the edge of a sword, prescribed for the virtuous?
Praiseworthy is the renunciation in his hands; devotion to the feet of the Guru upon his head; truthful speech in his mouth; incomparable valor in his victorious arms;
a pure disposition in his heart; and sacred learning attained by his ears.
Even without sovereign power, this is the ornament of those of great nature. (BharŚt 1.65)
In times of prosperity, the minds of the great become as delicate as a lotus;
and in times of adversity, they are like the stone of a massive mountain.
It is harsh with the sound of clashing together.
Water resting on heated iron is not even known by name;
that very same water, when placed upon a lotus leaf, shines with the form of a pearl;
and when fallen into a sea-oyster during the month of Svāti, it becomes a pearl.
Generally, one's quality—whether inferior, middling, or superior—is born from association. (BharSt 1.67)
He is a son who pleases his father with virtuous deeds;
she is a wife who desires only the welfare of her husband;
and he is a friend whose conduct remains equal in both adversity and prosperity.
These three things in the world are obtained by those who have performed meritorious deeds.
There is but one deity, whether Keśava or Śiva;
there is but one friend, whether a king or an ascetic;
and there is but one dwelling, whether in a city or in a forest.
For indeed, a wife is either beautiful or a cave. (BharSt 1.69)
Exalting themselves through humility while proclaiming their own virtues by speaking of the merits of others,
they accomplish their own purposes through efforts of vast and ever-expanding undertakings for the sake of others;
and by means of patience alone, they neutralize the wicked whose mouths are clamorous with harsh words of insult.
Whom among the virtuous, whose conduct is full of wonder, would not be honored in this world? (BharSt 1.70)
Trees are bent by the emergence of fruit; clouds hang low with fresh waters;
and virtuous men remain humble amidst their prosperities.
This is the very nature of those who assist others. (BharSt 1.71)
The ear of those devoted to compassion shines through learning alone, not by earrings; the hand shines through giving, not by bracelets; and the body shines through these very acts.
Not by means of sandalwood, but through acts of benefiting others.
He restrains one from evil, joins one with what is beneficial, conceals secrets, and makes virtues manifest;
he does not abandon one who has fallen into calamity and gives at the proper time.
The virtuous proclaim this to be the characteristic of a true friend. (BharSt 1.73)
The sun causes the lotus pond to bloom; the moon causes the circle of night-lilies to open;
and even the cloud gives water without being entreated.
The virtuous have themselves undertaken the exertion for the welfare of others.
Some noble beings, striving for the sake of others, renounce their own self-interest;
those who exert themselves for the sake of others without contradicting their own interest are merely ordinary;
but those who destroy the welfare of others for their own benefit—these are human rākṣasas.
But as for those who pointlessly destroy the welfare of others—who are they that we do not know?

Indeed, all your virtues were formerly given to the water that had entered into you; then, perceiving the heat of the milk, that water offered its own self into the fire. Upon seeing the calamity of its friend, it became intent on going into the fire itself.
By that water, fire is extinguished; but the friendship of the virtuous is of such a nature as this.
Here sleeps Keśava; here lie the hosts of his enemies; here rest the multitudes of mountain peaks seeking refuge;
and here also is the submarine fire along with all the fires of universal destruction.
Oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight is the form of the ocean!

Cut off craving, cultivate patience, abandon pride, and take no delight in evil. Speak the truth, follow the path of the virtuous, and serve wise people. Honor those worthy of respect, conciliate even your enemies, and proclaim your humility.
Protect your reputation; show compassion to the suffering—this is the conduct of the virtuous.
With their minds, speech, and bodies filled with the nectar of merit, they delight the three worlds with series of benefactions,
constantly magnifying even the smallest atoms of others' virtues into mountains.
O virtuous ones, how few are the saints who blossom within their own hearts! (BharSt 1.79)
Of what use is that mountain of gold or that mountain of silver, when the trees that grow upon them are merely trees?
We consider only the Malaya mountain to be truly such, by virtue of the shelter it provides.
Kaṅkola, nimba, and kaṭuja are also considered types of sandalwood.
The gods were not satisfied with precious jewels, nor did they experience fear from the terrible poison; yet,
without the nectar of immortality, they found no rest.
The wise do not desist from that which they have determined to be the truth.
At times sleeping on the bare ground, and at others reclining on a royal couch;
at times subsisting on vegetables, and at others relishing rice with ghee; at times wearing a patched garment, and at others clad in celestial raiment.
A person of intelligence who seeks to accomplish his purpose takes account neither of suffering nor of pleasure.

Goodness of character is the ornament of power; restraint of speech is that of heroism; tranquility is that of knowledge; humility is that of learning; expenditure on worthy recipients is that of wealth;
freedom from anger is that of austerity; forgiveness is that of a ruler; and freedom from hypocrisy is that of dharma.
For all people, this morality is the supreme ornament and the cause of everything.
Let those skilled in policy revile me, or let them praise me;
let Fortune enter me, or let her depart as she pleases;
let death come this very day, or at the end of an eon.
The wise do not take even a single step away from the path that is right.
With his hopes shattered, his body shriveled like a basket, and his senses withered by hunger,
a rat made a hole at night and fell of its own accord into the mouth of a serpent;
satisfied by that serpent's flesh, it quickly departed by the very same way it had come.
O people, behold that fate alone is indeed the cause of the rise and fall of men. (Bharata Śataka 1.85)
For laziness is the great enemy residing within the bodies of men;
there is no kinsman equal to diligence.
Acting thus, one does not come to grief.
"The moon, though severed, grows again; though waned, it increases once more.
Reflecting thus, the virtuous do not suffer amidst miseries.

Though he was endowed with such sovereignty and power— having Bṛhaspati as his leader, the thunderbolt as his weapon, the gods as his soldiers, heaven as his fortress, and Airāvata the elephant as his mount— the slayer of Bala was nevertheless shattered by his enemies in battle.
Therefore, it is clear that destiny alone is the refuge; fie, fie upon futile human effort! (BharSt 1.88)
The fruit of human beings depends on their karma,
and the intellect follows the course of karma; nevertheless, one should cultivate a wise mind.
Only by acting after having thoroughly investigated.
Indeed, having been struck on the head by the rays of the sun,
he sought a place free from heat and, by the power of fate, went to the foot of a palm tree;
even there, his head was broken with a loud noise by a large fruit falling upon him.
Generally, wherever one who is devoid of fortune goes, there too misfortunes follow.
Having observed the affliction of the sun and moon by the planets, the captivity of even elephants and serpents, and the poverty of those possessed of wisdom—
"Alas, destiny is powerful; such is my thought. (Bharata Śataka 1.91)
He first creates a jewel among men, a source of all virtues and an ornament of the earth;
yet even that he causes to perish in an instant.
Alas, how painful! How unwise is the Creator! (BharŚt 1.92)
When there is no leaf at all on the *karīra* shrub, what is the fault of spring?
If even the owl does not look about during the day, what is the fault of the sun?
When no drops of rain fall into the mouth of the *cātaka* bird, what is the fault of the cloud?
Who is capable of wiping away that which was previously inscribed on the forehead by destiny? (BharSt 1.93)

We pay homage to the gods; yet surely even they are subject to the Destroyer’s decree. That decree is to be revered; yet it too yields only the specific fruit of past actions. If the fruit is dependent on action, what is the use of the gods, and what is the use of the decree?
Homage to those karmas, before which even Brahmā has no power.
By whom Brahmā was constrained like a potter within the belly of the vessel of the cosmic egg; by whom Viṣṇu was cast into the great peril of the thicket of his ten incarnations;
and by whom Rudra was made to wander for alms with a skull-cup in the hollow of his hands—[to that Śiva, I bow].
The sun revolves eternally in the sky; homage to that action! (BharSt 1.95)
Neither physical form bears fruit, nor lineage, nor character; neither learning, nor service rendered with effort.
Indeed, it is only the fortunes accumulated through past austerities that bear fruit.
In due time, they bear fruit for a person, just like trees.
In the forest, in battle, amidst enemies, water, or fire, upon the great ocean, or on a mountain peak—
whether asleep, heedless, or situated in a perilous position.
Merits performed in the past protect them.
Worship that divine Satkriyā, who turns the virtuous into the wicked and the wise into fools, who makes benefactors hateful and renders nectar into deadly poison in an instant,
if you desire to enjoy your cherished fruit.
O virtuous one, do not in vain place your reliance upon vast virtues when they are beset by calamities.
Whether performing a task that possesses merit or lacks it,
a wise person should diligently consider the consequences;
for actions performed with excessive haste lead to trouble until their final completion.
The ripening [of that karma] is like a thorn, burning the heart. // BharSt_1.99 //
In a vessel made of beryl, he cooks sesame seeds with heaps of sandalwood for fuel;
for the sake of the root of the sun-plant, he plows the earth with golden plowshares;
having fashioned pieces of camphor, he seeks a livelihood here by sowing *kodrava* grain on all sides.
Having reached this land of action, that unfortunate person who does not practice virtue is truly wretched.
Let him dive into the waters, let him ascend the peak of Mount Meru, let him conquer his enemy in battle,
let him practice trade, agriculture, and service, and let him learn all sciences and arts;
let him even traverse the vast sky like a bird, despite making the greatest effort.
What is impossible does not come to be here; how could there be the destruction of that which is destined to be? (BharSt 1.101)
For him, the terrifying forest becomes a preeminent city;
all people become his own kin;
and the entire earth becomes filled with treasures and jewels.
For that man who possesses abundant merit from previous deeds.
What is gain? Association with the virtuous. What is misery? Association with those who are not wise.
What is loss? Transgression of one's commitments. What is skill? Delight in the true nature of Dharma.
Who is a hero? One who has conquered the senses. Who is the dearest? She who is devoted to her vows. What is wealth? [The Dharma].
What is knowledge? Not having to travel abroad. What is sovereignty? The fulfillment of one's commands. (Bhartrihari Śataka 1.103)

The earth was adorned here and there by those impoverished of unpleasant speech but wealthy in pleasant speech, who were content with their own wives and desisted from censuring others. (Bharata Śataka 1.104)
For even when one whose conduct is steadfast is treated with contempt, the quality of his fortitude cannot be wiped away;
it is like fire that has been turned face-downward— its heat remains.
The flame never goes downward at all.
The arrows of a beloved’s sidelong glances do not pierce his heart, the heat of the fire of jealousy does not consume him,
and abundant sense-objects do not drag him away with the snares of greed.
That steadfast one conquers this entire triple world.
For even by a single hero,
the surface of the earth is trodden underfoot,
just as it is by the sun.
By means of his vast and quivering splendor.
To him, fire becomes water; the ocean becomes a mere stream in an instant;
Mount Meru becomes a tiny pebble; the king of beasts immediately becomes a deer;
the serpent becomes like a garland of flowers; and the taste of poison becomes a rain of nectar.
In whose body there blossoms a character most beloved by the entire world. (BharSt 1.108)
Following his own mother-like modesty, which gives birth to a flood of virtues and possesses an exceedingly pure heart,
a man of spirit easily abandons even his life-breaths.
Those who are devoted to the vow of truth do not, however, violate their promise.
The Śṛṅgāra-śataka of Bhartṛhari:
[In which] Śambhu, Svayambhū, and Hara [are compared] to fawn-eyed women.
Salutations to that Blessed One whose banner is the sea-monster, who was adorned by conduct beyond the reach of words, and by whom houses, jars, and servants were constantly fashioned. (BharŚt 2.1)
With smiles and expressions, with bashfulness and fear, with averted faces and side-long glances,
with words, with jealous quarrels, and with playful gestures.
Indeed, women are a bond through all states of being. (Bharata Śāstra 2.2)
Glances with eyes slightly squinted through the grace of the eyebrows,
affectionate words, smiles ending in modesty,
and movements both slow and playful as she walks or stands.
This is both the ornament and the weapon of women. (Bharata Śāstra 2.3)

By these glances of the young maidens— charming with passion, sometimes with the knitting of eyebrows, sometimes filled with modesty, sometimes with great alarm, and sometimes playful and graceful— [the world was captivated].
The quarters of the sky appeared as if strewn with clusters of shimmering blue lotuses. // BharSt_2.4 //
Her face blooms like the moon; her eyes are capable of mocking the lotus; her complexion surpasses gold; her mass of hair outshines the swarm of bees;
her breasts steal the grace of the frontal lobes of an elephant; and her hips are heavy.
In young women, a charm of speech and natural gentleness are their innate ornaments.
The splendor of her gaze is charming with a slight smile and naturally tremulous; the movement of her speech is savory with fresh and playful expressions;
and the onset of her gait is accompanied by budding gestures of grace.
For what indeed is not beautiful in a fawn-eyed woman who is touching her youth?

Among all things to be seen, what is supreme? The face of the deer-eyed one, bright with love. Among all things to be smelled, what is it? The breath from her mouth. Among all things to be heard, what is it? Her speech. Among all things to be tasted, what is it? The nectar of her sprout-like lips. Among all things to be touched, what is it? Her body. And what is to be meditated upon? [Her very essence.]
What need is there for those with sensitive hearts to seek such charms elsewhere when they are present in fresh youth? (BharSt 2.7)
Whose mind do these young women not render helpless— their girdles of many tinkling bracelets and their anklets surpassing the cries of royal swans?
With side-long glances resembling those of a startled, innocent doe.
Her body stained with saffron paste, her necklace trembling upon her fair breasts, and her lotus-feet resounding with the tinkling of anklets like swans.
Whom on earth does a beautiful woman not bring under her sway?
Surely those excellent poets must have spoken erroneously who always say that women are weak;
for by the casting of their glances, with pupils rolling in agitation, [they bring even the steadfast to ruin].
Even Śakra and the other gods have been conquered by you; how much more so those who are weak?
Surely the god whose banner bears the sea-monster is obedient to the command of that fair-browed woman, since he acts upon those things signaled by the movements of her eyes. (Bharata Śāstra 2.11)
The hair is restrained; the eyes have reached the further shore even of the Vedas;
the interior of the mouth is strewn with swarms of teeth, pure by their very nature;
and these two jar-like breasts are beautiful due to the constant residence of pearls—thus [is she].
O slender one, even though your form is tranquil, it truly causes passion to arise within us.
O charming girl, what is this unprecedented skill with the bow seen in you, by which you pierce hearts with virtues alone, and not with arrows? (BharSt 2.13)
Though there is a lamp, though there is fire, and though the stars, the sun, and the moon exist, this world has become shrouded in darkness for me without that fawn-eyed woman. (BharSt 2.14)
This swelling mass of breasts, these tremulous eyes, these flickering creeper-like brows,
and this sprout-like lip overspread with passion— may they indeed cause me pain;
yet they are like a garland of letters of good fortune, inscribed by the Flower-Armed God himself.
Why does that line of hair, though situated in the middle, cause such excessive heat?
With a face like a moonstone, with hair as dark as sapphires,
and with hands like rubies, she shone as if composed entirely of jewels.
With her heavy breasts as Jupiter, her radiant moon-like face as the Sun,
and her two feet as Saturns, she shone like an assembly of planets.
If her breasts are firm, her hips alluring, and her face beautiful, O mind, why this agitation?
If you have a desire for them, perform meritorious deeds.
For indeed, without merits, one's desired goals do not come to fruition.
These [youths] possess the fresh fragrance of the beauty of youth; they are the onset of the prowess of mature sexual union; they are the sureties for the conquest of Love;
they are long-time thieves of the heart and the sole masters of novel transformations.
The playful activities of the fawn-eyed women triumph in some ineffable way.
Sweet with affection, overflowing with love, they have become the very essence of aesthetic flavor;
sweet in their speech, charmingly simple, and manifesting joy; naturally beautiful, moist with confidence, and bestowing the awakening of passion.
In private, certain casual conversations of the fawn-eyed women captivate the heart.
Resting again and again in the shade of the forest trees, a certain slender woman wandered about,
holding up her breasts with the edge of her garment.
She was warding off the rays of the moon.
When she was out of sight, we desired only the sight of her;
having seen her, we were solely intent on the pleasure of an embrace; now that the long-eyed one has been embraced, we pray for more.
The non-difference between the two bodies. (BharSt 2.22)
Mālatī on my head, yawnings in my mouth, sandalwood paste on my face, and a body smeared with saffron; on my chest, my beloved, languid with intoxication.
This remaining scripture is heaven itself. (BharSt 2.23)
At first she approaches me with a slight lack of passion; then her longing arises;
thereafter she becomes bashful; then her effort slackens; then her fortitude is destroyed;
then she is moistened by love; and finally, she becomes bold in the intense privacy of desirable dalliance.
The sexual union with a woman of noble family is delightful, its pleasure enhanced by the pulling of limbs without attachment.
Of those who had fallen upon his chest, with their braided hair disheveled, their eyes half-closed yet slightly opened,
and whose cheeks were perspiring from the exhaustion of lovemaking— of their lips...
The fortunate ones drink the honey of women. (BharSt 2.25)
That essence of divine love which shines forth following consciousness for those with eyes closed is perceived by each other as unmistakably real.
This alone is the eradication of desire. (BharSt 2.26)
This is improper and contrary to the natural order for men— that they should still experience the transformations of passion even in old age;
yet it is not so for women of shapely hips.
Life or sexual pleasure lasts only until the breasts fall away.
Indeed, no one in this world has ever reached the end of the ocean of royal craving;

what is the use of abundant wealth when youth, full of passion, has already faded from one's own body? Let us go home while we can, repeatedly assailing those women whose lotus-eyes are in full bloom.
The beauty of beloved women is not suddenly destroyed by old age.
It is the sole abode of passion, the cause for attaining the great suffering of the hundreds of hells, the seed of the arising of delusion, and a mass of clouds to the moon of primordial wisdom;
it is the singular friend of Kandarpa, manifesting a continuous stream of various evident faults.
For in this world, there is indeed nothing other than wealth, kin, family, home, and youth. (BharṛT 2.29)
In that ocean of the pearls of clever speech, which is a rain-cloud for the tree of love, a flowing stream of the essence of playful sport, a dear kinsman to Pradyumna,
a purifying moon for the cakora-birds of slender women’s eyes, and a treasure-house of the fortune of good luck;
Some fortunate person does not undergo transformation even when new youth has arrived. (Bharata Śataka 2.30)

In this essence-less saṃsāra, how could those of pure intellect direct their minds toward a heart whose fortitude is distracted by the stain of attachment to serving at the gates of the palaces of wicked kings,
were it not for these lotus-eyed women who bear the mass of radiance of the rising moon?
Young women with swaying girdles and waists bending under the weight of their breasts.

In this auspicious place on the Himalayas— where caves are inhabited by perfected beings (*siddhas*), where trees are crushed by the shoulders of Hara’s bull, and where the surfaces of the rocks are washed by the Ganges—
what wise person would allow their head to become soiled and withered by bowing down?
For women, whose eyes are like those of a startled young deer, would not be the weapon of Love. (Bharata Śāstra 2.32)
O Saṃsāra, the path to your end is not very far away,
provided that those women with intoxicating eyes do not stand as insurmountable obstacles along the way.
Grant to the forest does a mouthful of kuśa grass, whose stalks have the luster of bamboo and whose roots are severed by the edges of stones;
grant them also the leaf of the betel vine, as pale as the cheek of a young Śaka woman.
Or it may be torn from the young brides with the tips of their reddish nails.
All those sinful objects of sense-pleasure are essence-less and devoid of the flavor of renunciation; let them be loathed, for indeed they are the abode of every fault.
Nevertheless, on this earth, there is no merit greater than that which comes from the welfare of others.
And in this cycle of existence, there is nothing else as delightful as a woman with eyes like blue lotuses.
In this world, the fruit of desire is this: that two people should be of one mind;
for when desire is formed with another's mind, it is like the union of two corpses.
Casting aside stinginess and considering the matter at hand, may the noble ones speak this with propriety:
should the hips of women be served, or rather those of the mountains?
Of the playful women, smiling with passion.

In this saṃsāra, whose essence is a dream and which is as fleeting as a transformation, let time somehow pass for the wise— those whose intellects are delighted by the flood of the nectar-water of the knowledge of reality; otherwise, it passes for those who indulge in the dense, expansive enjoyment of the breasts and hips of charming women.
Of those whose efforts at the playful touch of their palms were rendered futile upon the broad surfaces of their thick thighs.
Make your dwelling either in the waters of the Gaṅgā, which take away sin,
or on the two breasts of a young woman, which are captivating and full of charm.
What is the use of many fruitless and senseless prattlings here? Men in this world should always pursue two things:
the fresh, intoxicating playfulness of beautiful women, and [the teachings of] the Buddha.
Whether it be youth, exhausted by the weight of the breasts, or the forest; Bhārata 2.39.
I speak the truth, not out of partiality; this is the reality even throughout the seven worlds: there is nothing else as captivating as women with shapely hips.
And there is nothing else that is the sole cause of suffering. (BharSt 2.40)

Seeing her, even a wise man becomes intoxicated, rejoices, finds delight, and offers praise, thinking: "She is lovely; she has lotus-eyes; she has broad hips; she has rising, full, and lofty breasts; she has a face like a lotus; she has beautiful brows."
Alas, what a wicked act of delusion is this—to regard as desirable a woman who is a visibly impure leather bag! (BharSt 2.41)
When remembered, she causes torment; when seen, she brings about madness;
when touched, she leads to delusion—how indeed can she be called a beloved? (BharSt 2.42)
As long as she remains within the range of vision, she consists of nectar;
but once she has passed from the path of the eyes, she exceeds even poison.
There is neither nectar nor poison whatsoever apart from this woman of shapely hips;
she alone, when in love, is the creeper of nectar, but when devoid of passion, she is the vine of poison.
It is an eddy of doubts, a city of immodesty, a stronghold of rashness, a repository of faults, a field consisting of a hundred deceits, and a source of distrust;
it is an obstacle to the gate of heaven, the gateway to the city of hell, and a casket for all illusions.
By whom was this female mechanism created—this poison consisting of nectar, the snare for the world of living beings? (BharSt 2.45)
This moon has not become her face by virtue of truth, nor has the pair of blue lotuses attained the state of her eyes, nor has her slender body been fashioned from gold;
rather, poets have thus deceived the mind, even though one knows the reality.
Foolish people frequent the bodies of fawn-eyed women, which are composed only of skin, flesh, and bone.
The innate graces of playful women flash only in the heart of a fool;
for passion is indeed established by nature in the lotus.
The six-legged bee merely wanders about in vain. // BharSt_2.47 //
They delude, they intoxicate, they mock, they revile, they delight, and they despond;
having entered these, they take pity on the hearts of men.
What indeed do women with beautiful eyes not do?
This supreme lotus-face of the slender-limbed one, which steals the splendor of the full moon and possesses a noble form— wherein indeed dwells the honey of the lower lip—
is it now merely the fruit of a tree that has ripened, once its excessive sweetness has passed away?
In due time, it will become a source of unhappiness, like poison.
This river, bearing the form of a beloved woman— wherein the undulating waves of her three folds of skin are visible,
the pair of her high and full breasts are like a rising pair of ruddy geese, and she shines with the lotus of her face— is cruel throughout and pays no heed to anyone here.
If it leads to immersion in the ocean of saṃsāra, then let it be abandoned from afar.
They converse with one man, look with amorous glances at another, and think of someone else entirely within their hearts; indeed, who can truly be called a lover to women? (Bhartrihari 2.50)
Honey dwells in the speech of women, but in their hearts there is only hālāhala poison;
for this very reason, the lower lip is drunk and the heart is struck with fists.
Withdraw, my friend, far away from this serpent that is a woman— naturally treacherous, bearing the hood of her charms, and possessing the fiery poison of her sidelong glances.
One bitten by an ordinary snake can be treated with medicines, but [this one cannot].
For ministers are indeed devoured by those who enjoy women.
In this ocean of existence, the fisherman who is the god of love has cast out a hook called "woman"; by means of it, mortals who are greedy for the bait of her lower lip will soon be caught.
Having dragged out the fish, she cooks them in the fire of passion.
O traveler of the mind, do not wander in the forest of a passionate woman’s body, which is difficult to traverse due to the mountains of her breasts; for there dwells the thief of passion.
I was seen by a serpent— long, flickering, moving with a curved gait, radiant, coiled, and possessing the luster of a blue lotus— but not by his eyes.
When one is seen [by such], physicians are found in every direction, for they generally seek to save lives.
For one who has been gazed upon by those with charming eyes, there is indeed neither physician nor medicine for me.

For here, indeed, the senses— deprived of the supreme reality— are led astray by the thought: "This is sweet song, this is dance, this is its flavor, this fragrance is wafting, and this is the touch of breasts."
I have been deceived by these five rogues who act only for their own benefit.
It is not accessible to mantras, nor does it fall within the domain of medicine,
nor does it undergo destruction through hundreds of various pacifying rites; yet,
due to the onset of delusion, it repeatedly inflicts some kind of fracture upon the body.
This epilepsy of passion causes the vision to wander and the head to reel.
To one who is blind from birth, to one with a foul countenance, to one decayed by old age with limbs grown callous,
to a rustic villager, to one of low birth, and to one overcome by trickling leprosy—
to these she gave her own captivating form, out of faith in even a tiny fraction of its beauty.
Who would take pleasure in courtesans, who are like the withered creepers of the tree of discernment? (BharSt 2.58)
This courtesan is a flame of passion, increased by the fuel of her beauty,
wherein lovers are offered as oblations.
Youth and riches as well. // BharSt_2.59 //

What noble man would kiss the sprout-like lip of a courtesan, however charming it may be, for it is but a spittoon for the spittle of mercenaries, thieves, servants, actors, and lechers? (Bhartr̥hari Śatakatraya 2.60)
Blessed indeed are those [who behold] women with long, white eyes,
whose full breasts are thick with the pride of youth,
and upon whose slender waists the creeper-like triple folds shine.
Upon seeing such a form, the minds of those [others] undergo a transformation.
O child, why are these slow, playful, half-closed glances cast [at me]? Desist, desist! This effort of yours is in vain.
Now we are others; childhood has ceased, and our resolve is fixed upon the forest's edge.
Delusion being exhausted, we regard the web of the world as if it were a blade of grass. (BharŚt 2.62)
"This young girl incessantly casts her eyes, which possess the luster of blue lotus petals, toward me; what does she intend?
Our delusion has vanished due to the fever caused by the impact of the arrows of the hunter Smara."
The flame has been extinguished, yet even that wretched thing does not cease.
O Kandarpa, why do you weary yourself by twanging your bow?
O cuckoo, why do you prattle in vain with your soft and melodious notes? O charming girl, enough with these restless side-glances, so affectionate, clever, beautiful, and sweet!
The mind exists as nectar through meditation on the feet of the Moon-crested Lord, which have been kissed by his consciousness.
Indeed, for those whose minds are united, there is union even in separation; yet,
if the heart itself is divided, [there is no meeting].
The word *saṅgin* specifies the absence [of connection]. (BharSt 2.65)
"What is the use of going if she does not live?
And even if my beloved still breathes, what then?"—
thus [he thought], gazing at the garland of fresh clouds.
The traveler does not go to his own home. // BharSt_2.66 //
O wise ones, desist from the company of women, which offers but momentary and fleeting pleasure; instead, cultivate the company of the brides of compassion, loving-kindness, and wisdom.
Indeed, in hell, there is no circle of firm breasts adorned with pearl necklaces.
Or else, let her take refuge in the orb of her hips, adorned with a girdle of tinkling jewels.

When the uninterrupted friendship between the self and the mind of that adept— both emaciated by their devotion to the practice of yoga— shines forth, what need has he for the chatter of beloveds, the honey of their lips, or the moon-like faces?
With the fragrances of sighs and with the delights of sexual union involving the embrace of jar-like breasts.
When there was ignorance produced by the wandering darkness of passion,
then this entire world was seen as consisting of women;
now, for us who possess the salve of most acute discernment, [it is seen otherwise].
When the vision has become equanimous, one regards even the three worlds as Brahman.
This lamp of stainless discernment flashes forth even for the accomplished only so long as it does not [shine] before those with the eyes of a deer.
And she is struck by the flickering glances from the corners of her eyes.
The talk regarding the renunciation of attachment found in the mouths of scholars who are eloquent with the Vedas exists only in words;
[for them,] the hips are adorned with a girdle of knots of red gems.
Who is capable of abandoning women whose eyes are like blue lotuses? // BharSt_2.71 //
That false scholar who censures young women is a deceiver of both himself and others,
because even the fruit of asceticism [is lost].
Heaven, and even the apsarases within heaven.
On this earth there are some steadfast men who can split the temples of intoxicated elephants, and they are also skilled in slaying even the fierce king of beasts;
yet, I speak boldly before those who are powerful.
Rare are those men who can shatter the pride of Kandarpa.
A man remains on the path of righteousness only so long, and only so long does he exercise mastery over his senses; only so long does he maintain modesty and likewise uphold discipline—
until these blue-lashed arrows, drawn and released from the bow of the eyebrows, reach the path of his ears.
As long as the arrows of the glance, which steal away one's composure, do not fall upon the hearts of playful women.
To place any obstacle against that which women undertake through the impetuosity of intoxicated love—
Even Brahmā, indeed, is timid.
Greatness, scholarship, nobility of birth, and discernment exist only so long as [the fire] does not blaze within one's limbs.
The fire of the five-arrowed one has been extinguished.
Even one who knows the scriptures, possesses excellent offspring, and is free from extreme affliction is rare indeed in this saṃsāra as a vessel for the good destinies;
for [ignorance] stands here, flinging open the gates to the city of hell.
The creeper-like brow of beautiful-eyed women becomes curved like a key.
Emaciated, one-eyed, lame, and deprived of ears; with a missing tail, wounded, and drenched in pus; his body covered by hundreds of swarms of worms;
wasted by hunger, decrepit, with his neck fixed upon the rim of a broken potsherd.
A dog follows after a dead dog, and yet passion surely strikes even the slain. (Bharata Śataka 2.78)
Those fools of perverted intellect, seeking false fruits, who abandon the female consort (strī-mudrā) of the Flower-Armed One— which is victorious and bestows the perfection of all aims—
are struck down by that very same [consort] with extreme ruthlessness, stripped naked and shorn bald.
Some have their hair tied in five tufts, others are matted-haired ascetics, and still others are Kāpālikas.
Even Viśvāmitra, Parāśara, and others— who subsisted on air, water, and leaves— fell into delusion merely upon seeing the lovely lotus-face of a woman;
what then need be said of those men who eat rice with ghee, along with milk and curd?
If there were restraint of the senses, even the Vindhya mountains would float upon the ocean.
The winds bear fragrances; the tips of branches possess new sprouts;
the female cuckoos are filled with sweet yet piteous longing for their beloveds;
and the moon-like faces of young women emit sparse and faint perspiration.
When spring has spread abroad, in whom does there not arise an emergence of virtue? (Bharata 2.81)
This spring is sweet even with the sweet, melodious warbling of cuckoos and the breezes from the Malaya mountains; yet it causes embodied beings who are separated from their lovers to waste away.
Alas, in times of adversity, even nectar turns into poison.
The dwelling of one who possesses little is indeed as follows: by the side of his beloved, languid with amorous play;
the sweet warbling of the female cuckoo in his ear; a smiling bower of creepers;
a gathering with a few excellent poets; and the charming rays of the moon.
And for some here, the diverse nights of the month of Caitra gladden the heart.
Now, as she offers handfuls of flower-clusters from the mango trees as oblations into the fire of separation from her traveling husband,
the female cuckoos gaze upon her with longing;
for these birds too are wanderers through the air, drawn by the preponderance of the fresh fragrance of the *pāṭala* flowers.
The breezes from the sandalwood mountain blow, having caused the exhaustion and fever to vanish and become thin.
Let pride remain established in the hearts of affectionate women for as long as the sandalwood tree does not appear.
The Malaya breeze is fragrant.
In the far reaches of the quarters, swooned by the fragrance of the mass of filaments from the flowers of the mango tree,
amidst bees rendered utterly intoxicated with sweet honey.
In the spring, who would not feel longing?
The deer-eyed women are moistened with the exceedingly clear juice of sandalwood;
there are shower-houses, flowers, and moonlight; the gentle breeze, fragrant blossoms, and the pure roof-terraces of the palace.
In summer, they increase both intoxication and passion.
Garlands with heart-pleasing fragrance, the breeze from a fan, moonbeams, flower pollen, a pond, sandalwood dust, clear wine,
the pure lap of a palace tower, and thin garments for the lotus-eyed woman— these are the delights.
This shines forth in the summer season; those of virtuous deeds obtain it.
The abode white as nectar, the moon with its shimmering pure rays,
the lotus-face of the beloved, the exceedingly fragrant sandalwood powder,
and the garlands with their heart-stealing scent— all this [appeals] to a person full of passion.
It causes internal agitation, but not in one who is averse to contact with sense objects.
Her passion ignited by the appearance of a young woman, fragrant with the scent of blooming jasmine flowers,
she bore the weight of her high and full breasts.
Whom does the rainy season not bring joy? // BharSt_2.90 //

The sky is filled with gathering clouds; the earth is covered in *kandali* flowers; the winds bear the fragrance of fresh *kuṭaja* and *kadamba*; and the forest edges are delightful with the sweet, melodious cries of flocks of peacocks.
They cause everyone, whether happy or unhappy, to feel longing. (BharŚt 2.91)
Above, dense masses of clouds; across, even the mountains where peacocks dance;
and the earth, white with new shoots.
Where does a traveler cast his gaze?
Here is the play of lightning-vines; here is the wafting fragrance of the ketaki tree; here is the thundering roar of rising clouds;
and here is the sweet, melodious cry of the peacock’s play for those with long-lashed eyes.
How will these days of separation pass, when their intensity has been so fully gathered?
In the darkness where even the movement of a needle is impossible, amidst the thundering of mature clouds in the sky and the falling mass of raindrops— O you who consider yourself wise!—
this is but the golden and lovely play of the lightning.
And it spreads both joy and languor along the path for the beautiful-eyed women at their own will.

Due to the heavy downpour, it is not possible for lovers to go outside from their mansions; therefore, the long-eyed women embrace them tightly to ward off the shivering caused by the cold, while breezes cooled by spray arise, utterly dispelling their exhaustion.
Ah, for the fortunate, even a cloudy day becomes a fair day when they are united with their beloved.

Having slept half the night on the secluded roof of the palace, his limbs relaxed and weary from the exertion of impetuous lovemaking, he felt an unbearable thirst arising within him; devoted to the intoxication of wine,
he [drew] from a water-jar [water] that was free from the vine-like arms of his beloved, which had grown slack from the fatigue of their union.
One of meager merit does not drink the autumnal water, though its clear flow is enhanced by the moonlight.
In the winter, those who eat curd, milk, and ghee, who wear garments dyed with madder, whose bodies are thickly smeared with saffron paste, who are exhausted by various amorous sports,
and who are embraced within their homes by women with full thighs and breasts— [they do not suffer from the cold].
Fortunate are those who, their mouths filled with betel leaves and areca nuts, lie down in comfort.

In that season which bears the luster of fully ripened *priyaṅgu* flowers, where blooming *kunda* blossoms intoxicate the bees, and where the noble *mandāra* trees display their beauty as they sway in the cold winds—
those whose deer-eyed beloveds have not clung to their necks for even a moment, though she is skilled at dispelling the chill of winter’s frost; [for them, what is the use of this world?]
For them, the nights, equal in length to the watches of Yama’s abode, pass for the young.
Kissing the walls of their cheeks, producing whistling sounds at mouths adorned with curls,
causing the bristling of horripilation upon the weight of breasts beneath tight bodices,
and making the thighs tremble as they cause the garments to slip from the broad slopes of their hips—
Clearly, the wintry winds blow, filled with the conduct of libertines toward beloved women.
Disheveling her hair, closing her eyes, forcibly snatching away her garment, causing a thrill of horripilation to spread, and manifesting a trembling of agitation,
he repeatedly produced noble sighs and pressed upon her lips.
Now, this wintry breeze generally behaves like a lover toward beautiful women.
If one has no taste for something, there is no longing for it even if it is charming; though the moon is delightful and beautiful, the lotus does not desire it. (BharSt 2.101)
One wanders in dispassion, another roams in statesmanship;
someone else delights in the erotic—these are the mutual distinctions upon this earth. (BharSt 2.102)
May this be auspicious!
The Hundred Verses on Dispassion by Bhartṛhari.
Shining with a crest-lock that flickers like a beautiful bud of the moon worn as a topknot,
having playfully consumed the flickering moth of Kāma, and throbbing at the tip of his auspicious state,
he utterly dispels the mass of the boundless darkness of delusion surging within.
In the abode of the yogis, Hara, the lamp of knowledge, shines forth in white radiance. (BharSt 3.1)
I wandered through many lands, treacherous and difficult, yet obtained no fruit;
abandoning pride in my birth and lineage, I performed service as was fitting, but it was fruitless;
I ate in the houses of others like a crow, devoid of honor and filled with apprehension.
O Craving, you who are a harlot of evil deeds, you yawn with greed; even now, you are not yet satisfied.
The surface of the earth was dug up in the hope of finding treasure; the ores of the mountains were smelted;
the lord of rivers was crossed; kings were propitiated with great effort;
and nights were spent in cremation grounds with a mind intent on the worship of mantras.
O Greed, even a single blind cowrie shell has not been obtained by me; now, be fulfilled.
Harsh words were somehow endured by those intent on pleasing him; even laughter was suppressed within with tears, while the heart remained vacant;
and even the gesture of joining palms in reverence was performed by those whose intellects were paralyzed by the arrogance of wealth.
O Hope, you who are vain hope! What more than this do you make me dance?
For the sake of these lives, which are like water droplets upon a lotus leaf,
what have we not done, devoid of discernment,
before those wealthy ones whose minds are rendered senseless by the intoxication of riches?
Enough with these shames; even the sin of speaking of one's own virtues has been committed.
Forgiveness was practiced, not out of forbearance; the comforts of home were abandoned, not out of contentment;
the unbearable afflictions of cold, heat, and wind were endured, yet no austerity was performed;
wealth was meditated upon day and night by those whose lives were constantly at risk, but the state of Śambhu was never sought.
Whatever specific action was performed by those various sages, they were deprived of its respective fruits.
Wealth was not enjoyed; rather, we ourselves were consumed.
Austerity was not practiced; rather, we ourselves were scorched. Time did not pass away; rather, we ourselves have passed away—this is the nature of craving.
It is not we alone who have grown old; [the world] has grown old.
The mouth is overwhelmed by wrinkles, the head is marked by gray hair, and the limbs grow feeble; yet craving alone remains youthful. (Bhartrihari 3.8)
When it is opened by discernment and remains even, thirst subsides;
but when embraced by height, that thirst becomes excessively expanded. Wretched with its deep-seated grasping for the decayed sovereignty of old age, it is a vessel for thirst.
In which [state] even the lord of the Maruts comes to be.
The desire for enjoyments has ceased, and even pride in one's own importance as a man has dissolved; friends who were equal to my very life have suddenly departed for heaven;
slowly I rise with the aid of a staff, while my eyes are obstructed by thick darkness.
Alas, how deluded is this body, that it is still terrified of death and the states of woe! (BharSt 3.9)
Hope is a river whose waters are desires, turbulent with waves of craving; it possesses crocodiles of passion and birds of discursive thought, and it destroys the tree of fortitude.
It is exceedingly difficult to cross due to the whirlpools of delusion, profoundly deep, and its banks are the lofty shores of anxiety.
The masters of yoga, free from indolence, rejoice in that pure state which has transcended the other.
I do not perceive any wholesome conduct arising within saṃsāra;
as I reflect, the ripening of merits produces fear in me,
for even the sense-objects have been long held fast by great floods of merit.
The great arise as if to bestow calamity upon those addicted to sensual pleasures.
Objects of the senses must inevitably depart even after one has dwelt among them for a very long time;
what difference is there, then, in the separation when people abandon them of their own accord? For those who depart by their own will cause incomparable anguish to the mind.
For when these are renounced by oneself, they indeed bestow infinite bliss of tranquility.
Oh, those whose intellects are purified by the discernment of the knowledge of Brahman perform a difficult feat:

though they possess enjoyments, they renounce their wealth with absolute dispassion— wealth regarding which they have no firm conviction that it was theirs in the past, nor is it so now, nor will it be theirs in the future.
We are not even able to renounce that which we have grasped through mere desire. (BharSt 3.13)
Blessed are those who dwell in mountain caves, meditating on the supreme light; birds, lying fearlessly in their laps, drink the tears of joy that fall from them.
But for us, there is only the play upon the banks of ponds in palaces constructed by the imagination of our desires.
The lifespan of those who indulge in the pleasure of sporting in the forest is utterly wasted away.
A hundred morsels of alms-food, yet tasteless; a bed upon the bare ground once a day; as one's only attendants, one's own body; and for clothing, a patched rag made of a hundred tattered pieces.
Alas, alas! Even so, the sense-objects do not abandon him. (BharSt 3.15)
The breasts are merely knots of flesh, yet they are compared to golden jars;
the mouth is a house of phlegm, yet it is equated with the moon;
the hips, dripping and moist with urine, vie with the head of a noble elephant.
Repeatedly, the form made weighty by the distinguished among poets becomes an object of censure. (Bharata Śāstra 3.16)
Among those possessed by passion, Hara shines supreme, for he has taken half the body of his beloved; among those free from passion, no one excels the person who has abandoned attachment to women.
For other people are rendered deluded, pierced by the poison of the serpents that are the irresistible arrows of Smara.
The rest, tormented by desire, are incapable of either enjoying or renouncing sense objects. (BharSt 3.17)
Not knowing the nature of fire, the moth may fall into the fierce flame;
out of ignorance, that fish may also devour the meat attached to the hook.
But even though we here clearly perceive these things, we remain entangled in the net of worldly existence.
We do not abandon them; alas, how profound is the power of delusion! (BharSt 3.18)
When his mouth is parched with thirst, he drinks cool, sweet water;
when afflicted by hunger, he devours rice mixed with meat and other delicacies;
and when the fire of passion blazes up, he embraces his wife most firmly.
People mistakenly perceive the hunter’s remedy as happiness. (BharŚt 3.19)
A person deluded by ignorance, thinking that his lofty mansion, sons esteemed by the virtuous, inexhaustible wealth, a beautiful wife,
and fresh youth are all eternal, enters the prison-house of saṃsāra.
Having perceived that everything is momentary and fragile, the fortunate one indeed renounces it all.
If the wife is not seen at home— miserable, her tattered old garments constantly pulled by wretched children who, crying out in hunger, distress her for lack of food;
and [if she is not there] to speak words that dissolve into broken syllables due to a throat choked with stammering from the fear of a rejected request— then what is the point?
What wise man would say "give" for the sake of his own burning belly? (Bhartrihari, Śataka 3.21)
It is highly capable of severing the knot of cherished great pride; it is the brilliantly radiant moonlight that causes the lotus-cluster of the multitude of most weighty virtues to blossom;
and it is the axe for the spreading canopy of the vast, trembling vine of shame.
This belly-pot causes mockery, for it is so difficult to fill. (Bhartrihari 3.22)

In a holy village or a great forest, with his head shrouded by a white cloth and carrying a skull-bowl, he enters door after door— his vicinity blackened by the smoke from the sacrificial fires offered by Brahmins who possess the essence of righteousness— driven by hunger, seeking only to fill the cavernous pit of his belly.
A proud man is better off with his life than being in constant distress every day among those of equal lineage.
Have those places of the Himalayas— cool with the spray and droplets from the waves of the Ganges, and possessing beautiful rocky surfaces inhabited by Vidyādharas— gone to destruction?
Those humans who delight in contempt and the food of others. // BharSt_3.24 //
Have the roots perished from the caves, or have the mountain streams been destroyed by the peaks, or have the branches— laden with sap and clad in bark— been ravaged by the trees?
For such are the faces of the wicked seen when their courtesy has been forcibly stripped away.
Their creeper-like eyebrows dance under the influence of the wind of pride born from the meager wealth acquired with difficulty. // BharSt_3.25 //
Now, sustain yourself with merit-giving roots and fruits;
sleep upon the earth with beds of fresh leaves; arise, let us go to the forest, where there is always freedom from the base whose minds are deluded by lack of discernment.
Not even the name of those whose voices are faltering due to the agitation caused by loss of wealth or illness is heard.
In every forest, fruit is obtainable at will; there is water from the holy rivers, cool and sweet in various places, without fatigue;
and there is a bed of soft touch, composed of the tender sprouts of graceful creepers.
Even so, the wretched endure suffering at the door of the wealthy.

May I remember those days when I was among those who, before the Lord of Wealth, endured the sorrow of supplication, yet possessed minds content with the limited nature of sense objects; days when a smile would flash within their hearts.
When his meditation was interrupted, he sat down upon a bed of stones within a mountain cave.
For those who are continuously delighted by contentment, their joy is never diminished; yet for others, whose minds are fettered by greed for wealth, that joy is not destroyed by thirst.
Thus, for whose sake, from where, and of what kind would such a state of prosperity be ordained by fate?
Mount Meru, whose greatness as gold is contained within itself alone, does not please me.
Subsisting on alms is free from dejection and lacks worldly pleasure; it cuts through fear in every respect, grinds away all stinginess, intoxication, and pride, and destroys the flood of suffering.
It is easily obtained everywhere daily without effort, dear to the virtuous, and purifying.
The lords of yoga proclaim that this sacrifice of Śambhu is an inexhaustible treasure-house.

In wealth there is the danger of disease; in family, the fear of decline; in riches, the fear of the king; in honor, the fear of poverty; in strength, the fear of enemies; in beauty, the fear of old age;
in learning, the fear of disputants; in virtue, the fear of the wicked; and in the body, the fear of Death.
Every object on earth is fraught with fear for men; only dispassion is free from fear.
Birth is assailed by death; radiant youth by old age; contentment by the desire for wealth; the face of tranquility by the coquettish charms of mature women;
virtues by envious people; forest lands by serpents; and kings by wicked men.
Even prosperities are destroyed by instability; what has not been swallowed, or by whom?
The health of people is uprooted by hundreds of various mental and physical ailments;
where prosperity dwells there, calamities fall as if through open doors;
and death inevitably and swiftly makes every being that is born its own, rendering it powerless.
What, then, is the use of that unrestrained fate which has created this so very firm?
Enjoyments are as flickering as the breaking of high waves; life-breaths perish in an instant; the days of youthful happiness are but few; and the charm of beloved women is transient.
Therefore, having realized that this entire cycle of existence is utterly essence-less, the wise become enlighteners of others.
Let an effort be undertaken with a mind tender toward the welfare of the world. (BharSt 3.34)
"Enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds;
life is as fragile as water clinging to a cluster of lotuses tossed by the wind;
and the playful dalliances of youth for embodied beings are likewise transient"—having thus reflected, [one should act] swiftly.
O wise ones, apply your intellect to yoga, which is easily attained through the perfection of fortitude and meditative concentration. (BharSt 3.35)
Life is as fickle as a wave; the glory of youth lasts but a few days; wealth is like a mere mental construction; and the abundance of enjoyments flickers like lightning in the rainy season.
Even that embrace of a beloved, so tenderly offered by one with a beautiful face, does not endure for long.
Let your minds be fixed upon Brahman in order to cross to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
With bodies constrained, one dwells with great hardship amidst impurities during the stay in the womb;

in youth, enjoyment is made miserable by the turmoil of the pain of separation from beloved women; and old age is a dwelling place for the derisive laughter of beautiful-eyed women, while other virtues fail.
O humans, tell me: is there even the slightest bit of happiness to be found in this cycle of existence? (BharSt 3.37)
Old age stands like a tigress, threatening;
diseases strike the body like enemies;
and life flows away like water from a broken jar.
Nevertheless, that the world continues to act for its own detriment is truly strange.
Pleasures are of many kinds and their nature is fragile; it is by means of these very pleasures that this worldly existence persists.
For whose sake, then, do you wander here, O people? Enough with such exertions!
Let the mind be composed in meditative concentration, which is clear and brings peace to the hundreds of snares of desire.
If our word is to be trusted because of the arising of desire within one's own self, [then so be it]. (BharSt 3.39)

O friend, some are fortunate, having severed the entanglements of worldly existence at the edge of the forest; they have reached the state where the poison of the senses— the venom of mental affliction— is extinguished within their hearts,
and they find delight in the expanse of the sky made beautiful by the white moonlight of autumn.
Those who spend their nights taking sole refuge in reflecting upon the accumulation of their good deeds.
Established in which one regards the hosts of Maruts, headed by Brahmā and Indra, as mere particles of straw;
and through the savor of which even the sovereign powers of the three worlds, such as kingship, become tasteless— that alone is a certain supreme enjoyment, eternally arisen and expanding.
O virtuous one, do not take delight in those other enjoyments which are as fleeting as a moment.
That lovely city, that great king, that circle of vassals at his side, that assembly of clever men, those women with faces like the orb of the moon,
that exalted host of princes, and those panegyrical songs— [all were present].
Salutation to that Time, by whose power everything has come within the range of memory.
Where there were many, in some house, there now remains but one; and where there was once one, thereafter there are many, yet in the end not even one remains.
Thus night and day pass away, tossing them about like a pair of dice.
Time, skillful, plays upon the board of the world with living beings as its dice.
Life is diminished day by day by the rising and setting of the sun;
time is not perceived amidst activities heavy with the burden of many duties;
and though one sees birth, old age, misfortune, and death, no terror arises.
Having drunk the intoxicating wine of delusion, the world has become like one who is mad.

Thinking that this very night is once again that same day, living beings vainly run about, exerting themselves in those various activities they have already begun in secret; thus, by means of these repetitive and mundane pursuits, they are caught in such a cycle.
Alas! Though we are tormented by saṃsāra, we do not feel shame because of our delusion. (BharSt 3.44)
No meditation was practiced as a means to sever the cycle of existence according to the rules; nor was the Dharma, capable of splitting the door-panels of the gates to heaven, ever acquired;
and the pair of full breasts and thighs of a woman was not embraced even in a dream.
We are merely axes for the felling of the forest of our mother's youth. (Bharata Śataka 3.45)
The science befitting the disciplined, which subdues the hosts of adversaries, has not been mastered;
fame has not been raised to heaven by the tips of swords that split the frontal globes of elephants;
and the nectar of the lips of lovely women, tender as young shoots, has not been drunk at the rising of the moon.
Alas, youth has already passed away in vain, like a lamp in an empty house. (BharSt 3.46)
I have not attained stainless knowledge, nor have I acquired wealth; I have not performed service for my parents with a concentrated mind;
and I have not embraced beloved women with tremulous, long eyes, even in my dreams.
This time is being driven away, like crows by their greed for the food of others. (Bhartr̥hari, Śatakatraya 3.47)

Those from whom we were born have indeed long since passed away; those with whom we grew up have likewise been reduced to the realm of memory. Now, we ourselves are daily approaching our own downfall.
They have reached a state equal to that of the trees on the banks of a sandy river.
The lifespan of humans is limited to one hundred years; half of that is spent at night, and half of the remaining half is further divided between childhood and old age.
