What little remains is spent in the company of disease and the pain of separation, while the rest is consumed by service and other such burdens.
When life is more flickering than a flash of lightning, how can there be happiness for living beings? (BharSt 3.49)
For a moment he is a child, for a moment a youth devoted to the pleasures of desire;
for a moment he is destitute of wealth, and for a moment possessed of full prosperity.
With limbs worn out by old age, his body adorned with wrinkles, he is like an actor.
At the end of his wandering in saṃsāra, that man enters the merchant-town of Yama’s realm.
"You are the king, and we too are elevated by the pride of wisdom from having served our gurus;
you are renowned for your riches, while poets spread our fame in all directions. Thus, the difference between us two is exceedingly great in terms of our wealth of pride."
If you have turned your face away from us, we too are entirely free from desire.
You are the master of riches, and we too are masters of words; you are a hero insofar as your purpose extends, while our skill is inexhaustible in the task of quelling the pride of disputants.
The wealthy serve you, and those whose minds are free from the stain of ignorance desire to hear this [teaching] of mine.
O King, if you have no confidence even in yourself, then I certainly have none at all in you.
We are content here with bark garments, while you are content with fine silks; in this matter, our satisfaction is equal and without distinction.
But let him alone be poor whose thirst is vast.
When the mind is fully contented, who is wealthy and who is poor?
Fruit is sufficient for food, sweet water for drink,
the earth for a bed, and bark for clothing; yet for those whose every sense is bewildered by the drinking of honey from fresh clouds, there is no lack of immodesty.
I do not venture to approve of the wicked.
Let us eat alms; let us wear garments made of rags; let us sleep upon the surface of the earth—what need have we for lords? (BharSt 3.55)

Neither actors, nor jesters, nor singers, nor those skilled in the debate of the learned and the vulgar—what are we here to behold the king? We are but women, burdened by the weight of our breasts and immeasurable [in beauty]. (Bharata Śāstra 3.56)
In the past, this world was created by lords of vast hearts;
it was sustained by others and given away by still others as if it were a blade of grass.
Indeed, here in this world, other steadfast ones enjoy fourteen realms.
What is this fever of pride in men who possess only a few cities? (Bhartrihari 3.57)
Since not even a single moment has passed without hundreds of kings having enjoyed her,
what great esteem can there be among rulers for the mere acquisition of this earth? For they are but masters over a fraction of a fraction, a mere vestige of a limb of that [earth].
When sorrow ought to be felt, the dull-witted instead display joy. (Bhartrihari 3.58)
This entire mass of clay, though divided by the lines of water into many parts, is indeed but a single atom;
yet, having been partitioned into hundreds of shares, hosts of kings enjoy it.
What else can be said? Those who might give, or those who are giving, are themselves wretched and utterly impoverished.
Fie, fie upon those lowest of men who desire even mere grains of wealth from them! (Bhārata 3.59)
He was some extraordinary being born, upon whose head the enemy of Madana placed a white skull high as an ornament;
yet now, by certain men whose minds are intent on saving their own lives, [it is treated otherwise].
What is this burden of the fever of incomparable pride among men who are themselves bowing down? (Bhartr̥hari 3.60)
O heart, why do you enter that which is beset by afflictions in order to win the favor of others through various means day after day?
For when you are serene within, the multitude of wish-fulfilling gems arises spontaneously.
Does your solitary resolve not nourish that which you desire? (BharSt 3.61)
While the true river of the three worlds, which kisses the head of Śiva,
provides a virtuous livelihood through the bark and excellent fruits born of the *baṭa* tree,
who is this wise man who dwells in extreme misery due to the pain produced by the fever of calamity?
If he were not to show compassion toward his own family, he would indeed look like a face situated in a place of misery. (BharSt 3.61)
O mind, why do you wander aimlessly? Rest wherever you may;
whatever comes to be will be exactly as it is, and not otherwise. Without recollecting the past nor imagining what is yet to come, remain unreflecting.
I experience enjoyments through my union with them. (BharSt 3.62)

Therefore, desist from this thicket of sense objects which causes exhaustion; in an instant, take possession of the path to the welfare of the basis, which is skilled in the activity of pacifying all suffering, and abandon your own way of life that is as fickle as a wave.
O mind, do not again indulge in the transient delights of worldly existence; be at peace now.
Wipe away delusion and cultivate that delight in Him whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon;
O mind, embrace attachment to the banks of the celestial river.
For who can find stability in waves, in bubbles, in streaks of lightning, or in fleeting glories?
And the suffix *ca* is used after words meaning "flames," "serpents," and "the current of a river. (Bhartr̥hari, Vākyapadīya 3.64)
O mind, do not for a moment cherish this fickle Ramā with such attachment— she who is a courtesan in the business of wandering through the huts of the frowning brows of kings.
Having entered the gates of the city of Vārāṇasī, clad in a patched garment, [seek] the streets...
We look with longing for alms that have fallen into the bowl in our hands amidst the rows [of the assembly]. (BharSt 3.65)
In front is song, on both sides are poets full of flavor, behind is the tinkling of playful bracelets from the chowrie-bearers;
if this is so, then indulge in the craving for the taste of worldly existence.
If not, O mind, enter suddenly into the non-conceptual meditative absorption.
Prosperities that yield all desires have been attained—what more is there?
The feet of enemies have been placed upon their heads—what more is there?
Those who sought favor have been fulfilled with riches—what more is there?
If the bodies of embodied beings remain for an eon, what then? (BharSt 3.67)
Devotion to Bhava, the fear of birth and death residing in the heart, no affection for kinsmen, nor any transformations born of passion;
O Vijayā, you have created these forest regions, free from all defects.
What is there beyond this dispassion that remains to be sought? (BharSt 3.68)
Therefore, contemplate that infinite, undecaying, supreme, and radiant Brahman; what is the use of these false conceptualizations,
to which belong these worldly lordships, enjoyments, and the like?
They become objects of pity in the eyes of the world. // BharSt_3.69 //
O mind, through your fickleness you enter the netherworld, traverse the sky, and wander across the circle of the quarters;
yet even in your delusion, how could you ever find that which is pure and truly your own?
O Brahman, you do not transmigrate; rather, you attain liberation by means of that [knowledge].

What is the use of the Vedas, the Smṛtis, the recitations of the Purāṇas, or the vast treatises which yield as their fruit only residence in a hut within the village of heaven, and which are but delusions regarding ritual actions—
unless one abandons [all these] for that single [remedy]: the fire at the end of time that destroys the construction of the burden of the suffering of existence?
The attainment of entry into the state of the bliss of one's own self [is achieved] through the remaining occupations of a merchant.

"This is not the time for you; the secret must now be kept. If the Lord sleeps and sees you standing here, he will be angry"—hearing such words at their doors, O mind, leave them behind and go to the abode of the God who is the Sovereign of the Universe.
It is devoid of gatekeepers, free from harsh or cruel speech, and it bestows neither moonlight nor worldly comfort.
For when the glorious Mount Meru, enveloped by the fire at the end of the eon, falls;
when the oceans, the abodes of abundant makaras and crocodiles, dry up; and when the earth, though supported by the feet of the world-upholding mountains, comes to its end—
What need is there to speak of the body, which is as flickering as the tip of a young elephant's ear?
The limbs are shriveled, the gait has faltered, and the row of teeth has fallen out; vision will perish, deafness increases, and the mouth drools with saliva.
One's kinsmen no longer heed one's words, and even one's wife does not wish to serve.
Alas, what misery! Even a son acts like an enemy toward a man whose age is advanced.
Seeing the white color of the hair upon the head—
the very seat of the humiliation of old age— a man is abandoned and avoided by women as they depart, leaving behind him like a hundred bones piled up.
Young women avoid it from afar, as if it were a well belonging to a Caṇḍāla.
As long as this body is healthy and free from disease, as long as old age is far off, as long as the power of the senses remains unimpaired, and as long as there is no exhaustion of life—
during that very time, a wise person should exert great effort toward their own ultimate welfare.
When the house is already ablaze, what kind of effort is it to attempt digging a well? (BharSt 3.75)

Performing austerities, shall we dwell along the celestial river? Or, being noble in virtue, shall we devotedly serve our wives? Or shall we drink the floods of scripture and the nectar-like essence of various poetic works?
We do not know what we should do, for people have but a few moments of life remaining.
These rulers of the earth, with minds as fickle as horses, are difficult to propitiate; yet we are of gross desires, our minds fixed upon a very great fruit.
Old age seizes the body, and death takes away this beloved life.
"Friend, for a wise man there is no other good in this world than austerity."
When pride has withered, wealth has been depleted, the supplicant has departed empty-handed, kinsmen have wasted away, attendants have left, youth has slowly vanished, and all else is lost—
for the wise, the only appropriate course is this: to rest upon the crest of a mountain peak purified by the waters of the daughter of Jahnu.
In some places, his dwelling is in the caves, slopes, and groves of the king of mountains.
Beautiful are the rays of the moon; beautiful is the grassy woodland floor; beautiful is the happiness arising from meeting with the virtuous; beautiful are the stories in poetry;
and beautiful is the face of the beloved, tremulous with teardrops born of anger.
When the mind has fallen into impermanence, everything becomes delightful; yet, once again, nothing remains so.
Is not a beautiful palace roof for dwelling? Is not song and the like pleasant to hear?
Or is not the joy of union with one equal to one's own life-breath for supreme delight?
Yet, [the mind is distracted] by the shadow of the flickering flame of a lamp tossed by the wind that extinguishes the wandering moth.
Having perceived everything to be flickering, the wise have gone to the edge of the forest.
O dear one, though we have searched these three worlds from the very beginning of saṃsāra, nothing like this has ever come within the range of our vision or the path of our hearing—
this which dwells within the heart of one intoxicated by deep-seated and hidden pride, acting as a goad for the elephant of the sense-objects.
The restraint of the elephant that is the sense organs serves as the sport of the tethering post. (Bhartrihari Śatakatraya 3.81)
This is wandering at will, eating without meanness, dwelling with noble ones, and learning— the fruit of which is solely the vow of tranquility;
while the mind’s movement is sluggish, even when reflecting for a long time upon external matters.
I know whose noble asceticism has reached this fruition.
Our desires have indeed withered, and that youth has passed away from our hearts; alas, the virtues within our limbs have come to fruitionlessness, being without those who recognize virtue.
What is appropriate? For powerful Time, the intolerant Lord of Fate, approaches all at once.
Alas! It is understood: apart from the pair of feet of the Destroyer of Madana, there is no other refuge.
Whether it be Maheśvara, the sovereign lord of the worlds,
or Janārdana, the inner self of the universe, I have no perception of any difference between these two realities.
Nevertheless, there is devotion toward the one who has the young moon as his crest-jewel.

Seated comfortably on some riverbank of the celestial Ganges, its surface whitened by shimmering, expansive moonlight during nights of profound silence, those weary of the vast expanse of worldly existence cry out with raised voices, "Śiva! Śiva! Śiva!"
When shall we reach that state where we are overwhelmed by a profusion of suppressed tears?
Mahādeva is his god, and this river is his celestial stream; the caves are his dwelling, and these very green woods are his garment.
Time is his friend, and this is his vow—a vow free from all dejection.
Or how much more shall we say? Let the beloved be the banyan tree itself.
Having surrendered all our possessions, our hearts filled with fresh compassion,
we remember the course of destiny in this saṃsāra, which results in such flawed transformations; thus,
in this forest of merit, we are bathed by the rays of the full autumn moon.
We shall spend the three watches of the night taking refuge solely in the meditation upon the feet of Hara.
When, dwelling in Vārāṇasī on the bank of the celestial river, wearing a loincloth and placing my joined palms upon my head, shall I cry out:
"O Lord of Gaurī! O Śambhu, destroyer of Tripura! O Three-eyed One!"?
"Be gracious," they cried out; "I shall pass my days as if they were but a moment."

In that [city], the practice of various kinds of feasting in gardens occurs as the most intense of austerities; wearing only a loincloth is considered fine clothing; wandering for alms is a source of immeasurable ornamentation;
and even the imminent approach of death arises as something equal to an auspicious occasion.
Alas, why do the wise dwell elsewhere, having abandoned that Kāśī?
O Enemy of Smara, having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā and having worshipped you, O All-pervading Lord, with pure flowers and fruits;
having fixed my meditation upon you, the object of meditation, at the foot of a stone couch within a mountain cave;
delighting in the self, subsisting on fruits, and devoted to the words of my guru—by your grace, [may I attain liberation].
"When shall I be liberated from suffering through service rendered to the Person whose hands and feet are symmetrical? (BharSt 3.88)
O Śambhu, when shall I become solitary, free from desire, peaceful, using my hands as a bowl, clothed only by the directions, and capable of uprooting all karma?
For those who offer their hands as alms-bowls, who are content with alms that are pure by nature,
who sit anywhere whatsoever, and who repeatedly behold the universe as a mere abundance of grass— though they do not abandon the body, they touch the realization of unbroken supreme bliss.
Through honey, someone who has become easily accessible by the grace of Śiva shall become a perfected one among yogins.
A loincloth worn out and tattered in a hundred pieces, a patched garment of the same sort,
a state of carefree indifference, eating alms-food without expectation, sleeping in a cremation ground or a forest,
wandering at will and without restraint, and a mind always perfectly tranquil.
And if there is steadfastness even during the great festival of yoga, what is the use of sovereignty over the three worlds?
